governing_philosophy.title: A Government That Does Its Job. Then Gets Out of the Way.
governing_philosophy.summary: Set the floor. Protect the commons. Regulate harm. Keep power honest. Otherwise, let people get on with their lives.
governing_philosophy.governing_rule: Set the floor. Protect the commons. Regulate harm. Otherwise, get out of the way.
governing_philosophy.method: Start with the material problem. Trace the mechanism. Publish the evidence. Cost the intervention. Use no more power than the problem requires. Measure the result. New information changes the conclusion? Change the policy. An election promise creates a presumption: keep it. If reality materially changes, explain why, show the evidence, and accept the scrutiny.

policies.title: Set the Rules for Data Centres
policies.summary: Welcome data centres and AI infrastructure where they benefit Victoria—but make major facilities carry the additional power, water, infrastructure and environmental costs they create, and subject them to transparent assessment and genuine community consultation.
policies.hook: A facility that can consume hundreds of megawatts should not be regulated like another warehouse.

key_points.description: Require large facilities to match material new electricity demand with additional renewable generation and firming or storage, and pay attributable grid connection and network-upgrade costs.
key_points.point: Bring new power with new demand

key_points.description: Prioritise recycled, non-potable and low-water cooling. Major facilities should not displace household or agricultural access to scarce water, and developers should fund infrastructure upgrades their demand requires.

Set clear scale thresholds for mandatory impact assessment and public consultation covering energy, water, noise, air emissions, traffic, emergency risk, land use and environmental impacts rather than treating hyperscale facilities like ordinary warehouses.
key_points.point: Assess major facilities as major facilities

key_points.description: Require containment of contaminated runoff and compliance with enforceable noise, air, waste and pollution limits, backed by regulator powers proportionate to serious or repeated breaches.

Keep major facilities out of inappropriate residential and sensitive locations and require adequate separation where impacts warrant it. Do not impose an arbitrary universal kilometre buffer where site-specific evidence supports a better standard.
Apply strong privacy, cybersecurity, resilience and data-sovereignty requirements appropriate to the sensitivity and criticality of the workloads hosted.
Require major facilities to report material electricity and water consumption and compliance data so promised safeguards can be tested against real operation.

policies.shareable_quote: Build the infrastructure. Set the rules. Make the developer pay for the costs it creates.
policies.design_rationale: This policy regulates measurable externalities rather than treating data centres or AI as inherently good or bad. Requirements scale with facility impact. It avoids a blanket moratorium and avoids arbitrary universal distance rules: siting, separation and mitigation should follow demonstrated risk, while genuinely major projects receive major-project scrutiny.
policies.system_interaction: Victoria already regulates data centres through the planning system and general environmental obligations, with some facilities triggering EPA permissions for activities such as significant on-site power generation. This policy adds a coherent state framework across planning, electricity, water, environment and community consultation rather than relying on fragmented case-by-case treatment.
policies.economic_logic: Data centres provide digital infrastructure, investment and capability, but very large facilities can impose substantial marginal costs on electricity networks, water systems, roads and surrounding communities. Requiring proponents to internalise attributable costs reduces cross-subsidy by households while allowing projects whose benefits justify their impacts to proceed.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Poorly designed rules could freeze useful investment, encourage accounting games around renewable procurement, or impose the same burden on small facilities as hyperscale campuses. Thresholds should therefore be measurable and technology-neutral; additional generation claims should demonstrate genuine additionality; and reporting should allow compliance to be audited.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Victoria's 2026 Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan already recognises data centres as essential infrastructure while introducing expectations around additional renewable generation and storage, network costs, non-drinking water and siting. Existing Victorian applications include facilities with ultimate power capacity in the hundreds of MVA, demonstrating why scale-sensitive rules are warranted.
policies.implementation_outline: Define major-facility thresholds using power demand and other material impacts; require integrated planning, water, grid, environmental and emergency assessments above those thresholds; establish transparent consultation requirements; set developer-pays rules for attributable infrastructure; specify additional-energy and water standards; and publish ongoing operational compliance data.
policies.cost: Low direct budget cost; regulatory and assessment costs should primarily be recovered from proponents.
policies.funding: Proponent fees and developer contributions should recover attributable assessment and infrastructure costs.

policies.title: Turn Trams into Surface Rapid Transit
policies.summary: Upgrade Melbourne’s strongest tram corridors as surface rapid transit: physically separate trams from general traffic where feasible, give them stronger signal priority, build safe level-access platforms, run frequent all-day services, coordinate feeder buses and close short missing links to rail and major centres where the business case supports them.
policies.hook: Melbourne already owns one of the world’s largest tram networks. Make more of it work like rapid transit.

key_points.description: Use raised kerbs, dedicated lanes or other physical separation on corridors where geometry and network impacts make it workable, instead of relying on paint alone.
Strengthen tram signal priority so upgraded corridors are designed around reliable passenger movement, while managing pedestrian and cross-traffic impacts.
Build safe level-access platforms and crossings as part of corridor upgrades, coordinated with Victoria’s existing accessibility backlog program.
Pair upgraded corridors with frequent all-day service and feeder buses designed around reliable tram and rail interchange windows.
Appraise short extensions that connect tram termini to rail stations, major centres, universities and employment—starting with Route 86 toward Plenty Valley Town Centre and the Mernda rail corridor.

policies.shareable_quote: The cheapest new rapid-transit corridor can be the tram line we already own—if we stop making it sit in traffic.
policies.design_rationale: Melbourne does not need to replace its tram network with a new mode to capture many light-rail benefits. On corridors with sufficient width and demand, existing tram routes can be progressively converted into surface rapid transit through physical separation from general traffic, stronger transit signal priority, accessible platforms, stop rationalisation where justified, high all-day frequency and timed feeder connections. The network should also be tested for short extensions that convert dead-end termini into useful interchanges. Route 86 is an unusually concrete example: the City of Whittlesea identifies extension from the current Bundoora/University Hill terminus to Plenty Valley Town Centre and the Mernda rail corridor as a very-high-priority project, with land already set aside along parts of the alignment. The principle is not to extend every line indiscriminately, but to prioritise missing links that materially improve network connectivity, catchment and access to jobs, education and services.
policies.system_interaction: Coordinate DTP, Yarra Trams, road managers, councils and bus operators corridor by corridor. Physical separation and signal priority affect road allocation and intersection timing; accessible platforms should therefore be delivered with the existing accessibility remediation program rather than as a separate construction cycle. Feeder-bus timetables and routes should be redesigned around upgraded tram interchanges. Proposed extensions should be assessed alongside the Finish the Network, Complete Neighbourhoods and Homes and Stations policies so new termini and interchanges become mixed-use centres rather than isolated park-and-ride nodes.
policies.economic_logic: A corridor upgrade can increase the value of infrastructure Victoria already owns by improving speed, reliability, accessibility and interchange rather than requiring an entirely new heavy-rail alignment. Short network-closing extensions can also create trips that the current radial network makes awkward or impossible. Appraisal should compare passenger time savings, reliability, additional people and jobs brought into useful transit catchments, interchange demand, accessibility gains, operating cost and disruption against both bus and heavy-rail alternatives.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Removing general traffic lanes or parking can shift congestion and affect local access, so corridor design needs traffic, freight, disability-access and business-loading plans rather than assuming road space can always be reassigned without consequence. Signal priority can also create unacceptable cross-traffic or pedestrian delay if applied as absolute priority at every intersection; use network-level optimisation and publish performance. Stop consolidation can improve speed while worsening walking access, especially for older and disabled passengers, so accessibility and catchment impacts must be explicit. Extensions can become expensive scope creep: require a business case and compare them with frequent bus connections before construction. Grade separation should be exceptional and evidence-led because tunnelling or elevated structures can erase the cost advantage of surface light rail.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Victoria’s Melbourne Tram Plan already identifies accessibility, efficiency, frequency, reliability, journey time and connectivity as network objectives, and Transport Victoria already provides conditional tram signal priority at many intersections. The policy extends those existing directions into a corridor-standard program rather than treating upgrades as isolated stop projects. The City of Whittlesea’s current Road and Public Transport Plan gives a Route 86 extension to Plenty Valley Town Centre a Very High priority, states that land has been set aside along Plenty Road, Bush Boulevard and McDonalds Road, and estimates improved accessibility for roughly 13,500 residents. Gold Coast light rail is a useful Australian comparator for dedicated right-of-way, accessible platforms, frequent service and rail interchange, but corridor outcomes must be tested against Melbourne conditions rather than copied wholesale.
policies.implementation_outline: Sequence 1: publish a corridor audit ranking tram segments by mixed-traffic delay, accessibility gaps, service frequency, interchange value and feasible right-of-way separation. Sequence 2: nominate an initial set of corridor packages combining physical separation where feasible, stronger signal priority, safe level-access platforms, stop consolidation only where access is preserved, and frequent all-day service. Sequence 3: redesign feeder buses around reliable tram and rail interchange windows. Sequence 4: complete business cases for short network-closing extensions, beginning with the long-proposed Route 86 connection toward Plenty Valley Town Centre/South Morang, and assess other candidates on the same transparent criteria. Sequence 5: where road geometry makes surface separation impractical and passenger volumes justify it, compare short grade-separated sections with surface alternatives rather than assuming either tunnelling or mixed traffic by default.
policies.cost: Corridor upgrades and extensions require route-by-route capital and operating appraisal; prioritise high-benefit upgrades before new mega-project commitments.
policies.funding: Stage corridor packages through the transport capital program, bundling accessibility, track renewal, signal and streetscape works where this avoids repeat construction. Publish business cases for extensions before committing construction funding.

policies.title: Deliver Accessible Public Transport
policies.summary: Turn Victoria’s known public-transport accessibility backlog into a funded construction program. Publish every non-compliant stop and station, set delivery dates, and stop commissioning broad studies where the barrier and remedy are already understood.
policies.hook: Accessibility is already the law. The missing part is delivery.

key_points.description: Create a public, machine-readable compliance map for train stations, tram stops, bus stops and major interchanges, with known barriers and funded delivery dates.
Move standard, known accessibility fixes into a multi-year construction pipeline instead of repeatedly commissioning broad feasibility or strategy work.
Prioritise corridors and interchanges where one inaccessible element breaks an otherwise usable trip, and coordinate accessible vehicles with accessible stops.
Require station, road, tram-corridor and interchange projects to deliver relevant accessibility upgrades by default unless a published technical reason prevents it.

policies.shareable_quote: If the obligation is known, the barrier is known and the remedy is standard, fund the work.
policies.design_rationale: Victoria already operates under the Disability Standards for Accessible Public Transport. The core problem is therefore not a lack of policy intent but the gap between the legal accessibility floor and the network passengers actually encounter. VAGO’s 2025 follow-up found only 29% of tram stops had level access and only 18% of tram services in 2023–24 combined a low-floor tram with a level-access stop. The delivery model should distinguish between known standard remedies and genuinely unresolved engineering problems. Where the barrier, obligation and standard fix are already known, fund the work. Where heritage, utilities, geometry, drainage or safety create a real unknown, investigate that specific issue rather than commissioning another broad plan.
policies.system_interaction: The program would sit across DTP, Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority, VicTrack, operators and road managers because accessibility failures often occur at the boundary between vehicle, station, stop, street and interchange. The compliance map should use one common asset register and publish enough information for passengers and Parliament to see whether a complete journey is accessible.
policies.economic_logic: Accessibility upgrades have real capital costs, but repeated planning without construction also consumes money while leaving the legal and service gap unresolved. Bundling accessibility into already-planned renewals and corridor works can reduce repeat mobilisation, design and disruption costs. Costing should distinguish routine standard upgrades from constrained legacy sites requiring major reconstruction.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: A delivery target can encourage agencies to maximise the number of easy upgrades while leaving high-impact difficult barriers untouched. Report both asset counts and complete accessible journeys. A second risk is pretending all sites are technically identical: some require genuine engineering, heritage, utility or property work. The policy should eliminate redundant broad study, not necessary project design. Accessibility also extends beyond mobility impairments, so physical compliance metrics must be complemented by wayfinding, information and communication access.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: The federal Disability Standards for Accessible Public Transport establish the legal accessibility framework. VAGO’s 2025 tram-accessibility follow-up found substantial remaining non-compliance and slow delivery, including only 29% of tram stops with level access and only 18% of services pairing low-floor trams with level-access stops.
policies.implementation_outline: Within the first year, publish the network accessibility register and identify the highest-impact barriers. Convert known standard upgrades into a funded five-year rolling works program, with annual construction targets and corridor-level sequencing. Require every major transport and streetscape project to state which accessibility barriers it removes and explain any known barrier it leaves behind. Use targeted engineering studies only where a specific unresolved constraint prevents delivery. Publish annual progress by complete accessible journey, asset type, expenditure and missed milestone.
policies.cost: Multi-year capital program; cost to be built from the published asset backlog and site-by-site delivery classes.
policies.funding: Prioritise accessibility within transport renewal and corridor programs, then publish the additional capital requirement for backlog remediation rather than relying on unfunded strategy commitments.
policies.change_summary: Initial publication: pulls existing accessibility commitments into a dedicated delivery-first policy focused on the DDA/DSAPT backlog and whole-journey accessibility.

policies.title: Open Government by Default
policies.summary: Reignite democracy through proactive disclosure: publish government information before people have to FOI it, and make meetings, contracts, decisions and representative access easier to see and scrutinise.
policies.hook: If the public paid for it, the default should be that the public can see it.

key_points.description: Turn routinely releasable information into standard publication instead of forcing repeated FOI requests.
Require clear constituency-access plans, regular community access and annual engagement reporting from MPs.
Link ministerial diaries, lobbyists, interests, gifts and major decisions in searchable, machine-readable formats.
When government changes a major policy or election commitment, publish what changed, why, and the evidence behind the decision.

policies.shareable_quote: Reignite democracy by making government visible before people have to drag information out of it.
policies.design_rationale: Victoria already has proactive-release guidance, quarterly ministerial diary disclosure and public registers. The policy makes those principles systematic: publish routinely releasable material by default, connect the registers citizens currently have to search separately, and make representative accessibility measurable without compromising confidential casework.
policies.system_interaction: Builds on the Freedom of Information Act, OVIC guidance, ministerial diary rules, lobbyist and interests registers, procurement publication and parliamentary standards. Privacy, Cabinet confidentiality, security and active investigations remain protected where lawfully required.
policies.economic_logic: Proactive publication can reduce repeated FOI handling and duplication, but the policy's primary purpose is accountability and lower information-access friction rather than a claimed budget saving.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Poorly designed transparency can expose personal information, prejudice investigations, compromise security or produce misleading data without context. Publication rules need clear exemptions, metadata, accessible formats and reasons for withholding.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: OVIC states that proactive release is consistent with Victoria's FOI framework and can reduce the need for formal requests. Victoria already requires ministers to publish stakeholder diary summaries quarterly, creating a baseline that can be made more timely and machine-readable.
policies.implementation_outline: Audit repeat FOI topics; create proactive-release schedules; establish contract and decision-record standards; shorten and structure diary publication; define constituency-access and annual engagement standards; and build a common public interface linking meetings, interests, lobbyists, gifts, grants and procurement where lawful.
policies.cost: Digital publication, records management and reporting costs require agency-level assessment
policies.funding: Government-services and integrity budgets

policies.title: Protect Whistleblowers
policies.summary: Strengthen Victoria's existing public-interest disclosure system so people can report serious wrongdoing without being destroyed by retaliation or procedural traps.
policies.hook: If exposing corruption can destroy your career, the system is protecting the corruption.

key_points.description: A good-faith disclosure made through a reasonable integrity channel should be referred correctly rather than losing practical protection through a procedural mistake.
Create an expedited independent pathway for dismissal, demotion, harassment, roster manipulation and other reprisals after a protected disclosure.
Fund confidential advice so prospective whistleblowers know where to report, how protection works and how to preserve evidence lawfully.
Review reinstatement, compensation, record correction and other remedies so a successful complaint can actually repair the harm done.

policies.shareable_quote: Reignite democracy by protecting the people willing to expose what power would rather hide.
policies.design_rationale: Victoria already has a Public Interest Disclosures Act. The policy strengthens practical protection rather than pretending the framework does not exist: clearer referral rules, independent advice, proactive reprisal protection, stronger remedies and coverage review for outsourced public services.
policies.system_interaction: Builds on the Public Interest Disclosures Act 2012, IBAC, Integrity Oversight Victoria, the Victorian Ombudsman and agency disclosure coordinators. It cross-links directly with police integrity and broader anti-corruption policy.
policies.economic_logic: Whistleblowing can expose corruption, misuse of public resources and safety failures earlier. The policy does not book speculative savings; its primary purpose is integrity, lawful administration and reducing the personal cost of reporting wrongdoing.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Protections must not shield knowingly false or materially misleading allegations, immunise a person's own misconduct or prevent legitimate management action. Confidentiality rules also need to preserve fair investigations and procedural fairness for people accused.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Victoria's Public Interest Disclosures Act 2012 already provides protections from reprisals and certain liabilities for qualifying disclosures. Current government and integrity guidance confirms protections against dismissal, discipline, bullying and discrimination, while excluding knowingly false information and legitimate management action.
policies.implementation_outline: Review the current Act section by section; create no-wrong-door referral rules; establish independent confidential advice; strengthen interim anti-reprisal measures and remedies; audit contractor and ministerial-staff coverage; and publish privacy-preserving performance data on disclosures and reprisals.
policies.cost: Integrity advice, investigation and protection capacity require detailed costing
policies.funding: Integrity and public-sector governance budgets

supporting_research.title: Whistleblower Protection in Victoria: Where the Current Framework Can Be Stronger

policies.title: Police Integrity and Independent Accountability
policies.summary: Pair effective policing with genuinely independent misconduct oversight, transparent use-of-power data, strong civil-liberties safeguards and procedural fairness.
policies.hook: Police exercise exceptional state power. Exceptional power needs exceptional accountability.

key_points.description: Serious police misconduct, corruption and major human-rights breaches should ordinarily be investigated outside Victoria Police.
Report stops, searches, use of force, complaints and outcomes with enough context to identify systemic problems.
Use body-worn cameras for accountability without treating them as authority for indiscriminate biometric surveillance.
Protect complainants, whistleblowers and civil liberties while preserving evidence-based due process for accused officers.

policies.shareable_quote: More trusted policing requires more independent accountability, not less.
policies.design_rationale: Neighbourhood policing and visible local police can improve accessibility, but greater proximity to coercive state power makes integrity safeguards more important. The policy pairs local policing with independent serious-misconduct investigation, transparent reporting, procedural justice and limits on surveillance creep.
policies.system_interaction: Builds on IBAC, Victoria Police complaints processes and Integrity Oversight Victoria. Serious police misconduct and corruption would ordinarily be investigated independently, with reasoned and reviewable referral rules. The police-specific framework relies on the broader Protect Whistleblowers policy so officers and staff can report wrongdoing without retaliation. The final model must be reconciled with the Victorian Government's current police-oversight reform process and any 2026–27 legislation.
policies.economic_logic: Independent oversight requires dedicated investigative capacity and data systems. The purpose is institutional legitimacy and lower misconduct risk rather than an assumed budget saving.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Weak resourcing can make nominal independence ineffective. Overbroad disclosure can compromise privacy or investigations, while poor process can also deny officers procedural fairness. Reporting needs context and denominators, and body-worn-camera policy must not become a back door to indiscriminate biometric surveillance.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Victoria Police currently accepts complaints directly and IBAC provides independent police-misconduct oversight. The Victorian Parliament's Integrity and Oversight Committee recommended stronger police-oversight arrangements in December 2025, including a dedicated police corruption and misconduct division. IBAC's 2024–25 annual report says its Focused Police Complaints team became permanent after a pilot focused on people at higher risk of police misconduct.
policies.implementation_outline: Legislate clear independent-investigation thresholds for serious police misconduct; resource specialist oversight; publish appropriately contextualised use-of-power and complaint data; strengthen body-camera activation, audit and access rules; protect good-faith internal reporting; and establish regular human-rights and disparity review.
policies.cost: Independent oversight capacity, investigation and reporting costs require detailed resourcing
policies.funding: Integrity and policing budgets, subject to statutory design

supporting_research.title: Police Integrity and Independent Accountability in Victoria

policies.title: Complete Neighbourhoods
policies.summary: Stop approving dormitory suburbs that lock residents into driving for basic daily life. New growth areas should permit local shops and services, provide safe access to daily needs, and have useful public transport operating as homes are occupied.
policies.hook: We don't care if you want to drive. We care if you have to drive.

key_points.description: Do not approve large residential stages that depend on future, unfunded transport and services to become functional neighbourhoods.
Tie occupancy stages to an operational public-transport plan with routes, stops, frequency, service span and identified funding.
Require safe walking or cycling access to groceries, schools, open space, childcare and local services using the real street network.
Permit neighbourhood-scale groceries, cafés, health, childcare, offices and services under objective nuisance and design standards.

policies.shareable_quote: We don't care if you want to drive. We care if you have to drive.
policies.design_rationale: The core problem is both sequencing and urban form. New suburbs can be legally planned years before the transport and daily-needs infrastructure that makes them function as neighbourhoods, while rigid single-use zoning concentrates shops and services into a small number of distant centres. That locks in car dependence from first occupancy. Our principle is simple: we don't care if you want to drive; we care if you have to drive. This is car-optional, not anti-car urbanism. The response is not to ban cars, remove necessary access or centrally plan every tenancy, but to make walking, cycling and useful public transport viable choices for ordinary trips. Permit more small centres around stops and stations and incremental housing diversity—duplexes, terraces, small apartments and shop-top housing—across serviced areas. Major stations should be neighbourhood centres with housing, shops, services and jobs nearby; smaller stops should sit in walkable catchments with compatible local activity where demand supports it.
policies.system_interaction: Amend the Victorian Planning Provisions, PSP guidance and relevant growth-area controls so new precincts cannot rely on large single-use residential catchments or a handful of distant activity centres. Coordinate land-use approvals with the Homes and Stations Code, transport planning, infrastructure contributions, councils and utilities. Permit compatible neighbourhood commerce more broadly, and require new rail stations and major interchanges to be planned as mixed-use centres rather than isolated transport facilities. Hazardous industry and materially incompatible uses remain separated.
policies.economic_logic: Car dependence pushes transport costs onto households and road capacity onto the public budget. Better sequencing can reduce the number of trips that have no realistic alternative, widen the set of viable local businesses and lower the need for later retrofit. Those benefits should be measured rather than assumed: household car ownership, trip mode, local-business formation, road congestion, service use and delivery cost all belong in the evaluation.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: The policy can fail if government approves housing against promises of future transport that remain unfunded, or if accessibility tests are satisfied on a map but not in practice because arterials, missing crossings or poor service frequency make the trip unusable. There is also a risk of over-prescribing private land use: government should set access and compatibility standards, not dictate exactly which business occupies each site. Some households will still prefer or need cars; the objective is choice, not compulsory mode shift.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Victorian growth-area audits have repeatedly identified inadequate public transport and the resulting pressure on roads and households. RMIT research has likewise found that outer and fringe residents are more car-dependent where public transport is poor, while car ownership is lower near reliable public transport. International examples from Japan and Singapore inform mixed-use and neighbourhood-service design, but the Victorian case for early transport delivery stands on local evidence.
policies.implementation_outline: Amend PSP and growth-area approval rules so major residential stages cannot proceed on the assumption that shops, schools and public transport will arrive at an unspecified later date. Require a staged delivery schedule for daily-needs centres, safe walking/cycling connections and operational public transport, with named funding responsibility and occupancy triggers. Around new stations and major interchanges, reserve enough land and planning capacity for housing, local retail, services and employment so the station becomes a centre rather than a park-and-ride island. Permit neighbourhood-scale commerce throughout the precinct under objective nuisance standards, use actual walking networks rather than radius circles, and publish whether each stage met its transport and service triggers before later stages were released.
policies.cost: Planning reform plus early public-transport service costs require modelling
policies.funding: Planning-system implementation and transport operating budgets, subject to staged costing
policies.change_summary: Clarified car-optional rather than anti-car urbanism: residents may choose to drive, but daily life should not require owning a car.

policies.title: Prevention First Public Safety
policies.summary: Make preventing victimisation a core public-safety function: safer places, earlier support, targeted problem-solving, proportionate intervention and independent evaluation.
policies.hook: The best crime policy is the harm that never happens.

key_points.description: Treat crime prevention as a core outcome across planning, policing, health, schools and local services.
Use evidence about actual problems and locations rather than broad suspicion of groups or populations.
Do not rely on indiscriminate stop-and-search, demographic profiling or default biometric surveillance.
Measure victimisation, reoffending, trust, complaints and cost rather than counting activity as success.

policies.shareable_quote: Prevent harm first. Use coercion when it is necessary, not because prevention was neglected.
policies.design_rationale: Punishment after an offence cannot undo the original harm. Victoria already uses neighbourhood policing and a Violence Reduction Unit, so the policy builds a coherent prevention framework across urban design, youth services, health, education and policing while keeping coercive powers tied to lawful conduct and demonstrable risk.
policies.system_interaction: Coordinates Victoria Police, the Violence Reduction Unit, education, health, youth justice, planning, local government and victim services. It does not replace investigation, courts or sentencing.
policies.economic_logic: Prevention may avoid downstream victim, health and justice costs, but savings should not be booked in advance. Programs must report credible outcomes and cost per outcome.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Prevention can become vague spending, predictive surveillance or net widening if risk factors are treated as proof of wrongdoing. Separate support from coercive powers and measure demographic and civil-liberties effects.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: The AIC National Crime Prevention Framework, WHO violence-prevention evidence, Victoria's Violence Reduction Unit and Victoria Police Neighbourhood Policing support multi-agency prevention. VAGO's September 2026 youth-crime review also demonstrates the need for credible evaluation.
policies.implementation_outline: Map existing prevention programs and funding, define common outcomes, establish privacy-preserving evaluation, and publish continue, redesign or stop decisions based on measured results.
policies.cost: Cross-agency implementation and evaluation costs require program inventory and modelling
policies.funding: Subject to budget process and program evaluation

policies.title: Problem-Oriented Policing
policies.summary: Concentrate policing and prevention on demonstrated local harms, micro-locations and repeat problems rather than indiscriminate enforcement.
policies.hook: Police the problem, not everyone who happens to live near it.

key_points.description: Use local data and community reports to identify recurring harms, locations and times.
Start with design, transport, licensing, outreach or targeted presence where those address the problem.
Do not use high-volume pedestrian stops as a default strategy; retain lawful stops where grounds exist.
Report the local problem, response and measurable result where operationally safe.

policies.shareable_quote: Target actual harm, not whole populations.
policies.design_rationale: Crime is often concentrated at specific places and times. Place-based approaches can reduce crime without treating every person in a location as suspicious.
policies.system_interaction: Extends Victoria Police Neighbourhood Policing and local safety plans, with non-police agencies involved where transport, planning, licensing or services contribute to the problem.
policies.economic_logic: Targeted deployment may use resources more effectively than broad enforcement, but gains must be measured.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Poor implementation can become over-policing, hide demographic disparities or displace harm. Track complaints, stops, displacement and community trust.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Campbell Collaboration reviews report modest reductions from hot-spots policing and negative individual effects from high-volume pedestrian-stop strategies. Victoria already uses geographically based Neighbourhood Policing.
policies.implementation_outline: Audit current practices, define a local problem-solving cycle, improve stop/search and outcome reporting, and evaluate displacement and trust.
policies.cost: Operating-model and evaluation costs require Victoria Police modelling
policies.funding: Within policing and prevention budgets subject to implementation design

policies.title: Safer Night-Time Precincts
policies.summary: Treat late-night violence as a precinct problem involving transport, venue management, lighting, crowd movement, health services and targeted policing.
policies.hook: A busy street is not automatically a safe street. Design the whole night-time system around preventing harm.

key_points.description: Align late-night transport, pickup areas, lighting and staffed interchanges with predictable closing-time demand.
Use assault, ambulance, hospital and licensing data to identify recurring micro-locations.
Test licensing and service interventions against local violence and health outcomes.
Plan queues, toilets, sightlines, lighting, active frontages, emergency access and transport capacity together.

policies.shareable_quote: Night-time safety is transport, design, health, licensing and policing working as one system.
policies.design_rationale: Nightlife precincts show why foot traffic alone does not guarantee safety. Alcohol, crowding, transport bottlenecks, venue practices and street design interact.
policies.system_interaction: Coordinates Victoria Police, liquor regulation, public transport, health and ambulance services, councils, planning authorities and venue operators.
policies.economic_logic: Targeted precinct interventions should be compared with blanket restrictions using safety, health, mobility and economic outcomes.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Blanket restrictions may shift activity without reducing harm, while weak venue or transport controls can concentrate risk. Monitor displacement and unintended effects.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: WHO identifies harmful alcohol use among situational youth-violence risk factors and includes urban upgrading, problem-oriented policing and alcohol measures among prevention options. Victorian safer-design guidance supports natural surveillance and safe routes.
policies.implementation_outline: Map late-night assault and health data, identify repeat locations, review transport and licensing settings, trial targeted precinct packages, and evaluate safety and displacement.
policies.cost: Precinct-specific transport, design and service costs require local modelling
policies.funding: Subject to precinct trials and agency budgets

policies.title: Youth Diversion and Early Intervention
policies.summary: Expand early support and consistent diversion for suitable low-level youth offending, while keeping serious violence on a separate risk and victim-safety pathway.
policies.hook: A teenager does not become safer because the system waits until the first serious offence to notice them.

key_points.description: Create voluntary referral pathways for school disengagement, family stress, mental health, housing and substance-use needs.
Use cautions and diversion consistently for suitable low-level and first-time offending.
Coordinate one case plan across youth, health, education, housing and justice services for credible escalation risk.
Risk factors can trigger an offer of help, not new police powers or punishment for refusing voluntary support.

policies.shareable_quote: Offer help early. Reserve the justice system for conduct that actually requires it.
policies.design_rationale: Diversion can reduce unnecessary deeper justice-system contact for suitable low-risk youth while early services address established risk factors. Serious violence and victim safety remain separate considerations.
policies.system_interaction: Builds on Victoria Police youth caution and diversion pathways, the Violence Reduction Unit, schools, health, housing and youth services.
policies.economic_logic: The objective is lower victimisation and reoffending, not simply fewer court appearances. Funding follows measured outcomes.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Programs can widen surveillance, duplicate services or fail to reduce harm. Strong counterfactual evaluation and clear privacy boundaries are required.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Victoria Police already operates youth caution and diversion pathways. Campbell Collaboration reviews generally find lower subsequent delinquency from police-led diversion for suitable low-risk youth than traditional processing, while VAGO's 2026 review shows weaknesses in evaluation of Victoria's existing prevention program.
policies.implementation_outline: Audit statewide diversion and service access, define serious-violence exclusions and victim-safety requirements, improve referral capacity, build multidisciplinary case management and independently evaluate outcomes.
policies.cost: Requires service-capacity, case-management and evaluation costing
policies.funding: Subject to budget process and program evaluation

policies.title: Neighbourhood Police Posts
policies.summary: Trial neighbourhood police posts staffed by familiar, fully sworn but ordinarily unarmed community officers in lighter uniforms, with voluntary universal introductions, local patrols, independent oversight and civil-liberties safeguards.
policies.hook: A police station does not need to be a fortress on the edge of town. Put local officers where people already are.

key_points.description: Put compact local police bases in selected stations, activity centres and civic spaces instead of relying only on large standalone stations.
Use posts as bases for neighbourhood officers, with rosters prioritising foot and bicycle patrols, local contact and rapid nearby response.
Make it easier to ask for help without turning neighbourhood posts into stop-and-search checkpoints or surveillance hubs.
Pair greater local police visibility with independent misconduct oversight and transparent use-of-power reporting.
Assign a consistent officer to each beat and attempt one brief, voluntary introduction at every household and business per contact cycle, respecting opt-outs and resident-led follow-up.
Trial distinct lighter uniforms and no routinely carried firearms for dedicated community officers, while retaining lawful police powers, defensive safeguards and access to equipped response teams.

policies.shareable_quote: Safer streets start with people, visibility and help close at hand.
policies.design_rationale: Japan's kōban system shows how small police bases can support neighbourhood patrols, first response and everyday public contact without replacing larger police stations. Fusion also draws on the relationship-building purpose of Japan's junkai renraku practice: a consistent, locally assigned officer should attempt a brief introduction at every household and business in their beat once per defined contact cycle, except where contact has been declined or opted out. The officer simply introduces themselves and asks whether the resident has any questions or concerns. The resident controls whether the conversation continues. No questionnaire, household survey, personal-information request or investigative purpose is attached. Victoria already has Neighbourhood Policing and a 2026–27 service direction of highly visible policing — 'more street than station'. The proposal adapts those principles to Victorian law while pairing greater police accessibility with independent accountability, transparent use-of-power rules and limits on unnecessary coercive contact.
policies.system_interaction: Neighbourhood Police Posts would operate as small bases attached to existing Victoria Police service areas and local Neighbourhood Policing teams. Dedicated Community Policing Officers would remain fully sworn Victoria Police members with ordinary lawful arrest and enforcement powers, but have a distinct, lighter, clearly identifiable non-tactical uniform and would not routinely carry firearms. Other defensive equipment, potentially including capsicum spray, would be determined through workforce consultation, training, operational risk assessment and use-of-force safeguards. Their protected primary duties would be neighbourhood contact, public assistance, foot and bicycle patrol, prevention and local problem-solving, rather than routine high-risk enforcement. Officers would assist in emergencies within their training and equipment limits and request appropriately equipped response officers where necessary. Full police stations would retain custody, specialist investigation, evidence, vehicle and other functions needing larger facilities. Posts could be co-located with stations, libraries or council facilities and use secure remote assistance where permanent counter staffing is not justified. Planning guidance would also strengthen existing Safer Design and CPTED principles around natural surveillance, active frontages, lighting, sightlines and accessible pedestrian routes.
policies.economic_logic: The proposal tests whether smaller local facilities and more mobile patrol time can provide useful neighbourhood presence without reproducing the cost of a full police station at every centre. Co-location and multiple post formats should be tested against capital cost, recurrent staffing, response outcomes and officer time spent in the public realm. No statewide saving is assumed before that work.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: A local police presence can become over-policing if success is measured through stops, searches or enforcement volume rather than safety and trust. A lighter uniform and no routinely carried firearm do not themselves guarantee accountability or safety: the trial requires clear dispatch limits, de-escalation training, protective-equipment standards, officer safety evaluation and reliable armed backup for higher-risk incidents. Community officers retain ordinary lawful police powers but must not be treated as substitutes for appropriately equipped response teams. Universal outreach must not become household intelligence gathering: no compulsory participation, routine household questionnaires, demographic profiling, inference of suspicion from refusal, or use of introductory visits as a pretext for searches or investigations. Residents must be able to opt out of future routine visits; only minimal coverage and opt-out records may be retained, with restricted access, defined deletion rules and no routine linkage to criminal intelligence. The trial must monitor complaints, use of powers, demographic disparities, privacy, accessibility and whether lawful users of public space are displaced. It must not become a vehicle for facial recognition or indiscriminate surveillance. Strong independent oversight is a core dependency, not an optional safeguard.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Japan's National Police Agency describes kōban as small neighbourhood police boxes used for patrol, first response, public assistance and local contact. Victoria Police's Neighbourhood Policing model already emphasises visible, accessible geographically assigned officers, while its 2026–27 corporate plan describes highly visible policing as 'more street than station'. Victoria's Safer Design Guidelines identify natural surveillance, clear sightlines and active public places as crime-prevention principles. UK neighbourhood-policing guidance also supports targeted visible presence combined with community engagement and problem-solving.
policies.implementation_outline: Select a limited mix of metropolitan, growth-area and regional trial sites using local crime, victimisation, calls for service, transport use, foot traffic and community feedback. Design compact posts with Victoria Police, accessibility and victim-support input; test staffed and remote-assistance formats; integrate them with existing Neighbourhood Policing and PSO/station functions; prioritise foot and bicycle patrols. Trial a dedicated, fully sworn Community Policing Officer role with a lighter, distinctive uniform and no routinely carried firearm, subject to safety assessment, workforce consultation, defensive-equipment protocols and clear backup arrangements. Protect time for local engagement rather than routinely redeploying these officers to high-risk enforcement. Assign each beat a named local officer, with a designated backup and continuity of assignment wherever practicable. Trial a defined universal contact cycle: one attempted introductory visit to each household and business that has not opted out, without selective targeting. The introduction is limited to the officer's name, local role, where and how they can be contacted, and an open invitation to raise questions or concerns. Residents may decline or end contact immediately without consequence; no unsolicited repeat visit within that cycle, and further contact occurs only on request, apart from the next cycle or separate lawful policing duties. Maintain only minimal, access-controlled administrative records needed to document coverage and honour opt-outs, separate from criminal intelligence. Publish matched-area evaluation covering contact coverage, public ability to identify and reach their local officer, trust, officer safety, complaints, demographic disparities, crime, victimisation, response, use of powers, deployment and cost before considering expansion.
policies.cost: Trial capital and recurrent costs require Victoria Police site and workforce modelling
policies.funding: Subject to trial design and budget process

policies.title: Homes and Stations Code
policies.summary: Allow duplexes, terraces, small apartments and local shops across serviced suburbs, and treat every major station as the centre of a mixed-use neighbourhood rather than an isolated transport node.
policies.hook: Build neighbourhoods where driving is a choice, not a requirement.

key_points.description: Allow duplexes, terraces, townhouses, small apartments and shop-top housing under clear statewide standards.
Plan major stations with housing, shops, services, jobs and safe walking access so the station is a destination as well as a departure point.
Do not approve major greenfield housing stages on the assumption that transport, shops and services will arrive later.
Use public land and a public builder where it performs well, while testing affordability obligations against site viability.

policies.shareable_quote: Let more homes exist where the trains already go, and let more neighbourhoods offer a choice of homes.
policies.design_rationale: Housing reform should increase both housing supply and practical access. The goal is car-optional, not anti-car urbanism: we don't care if people want to drive; we care if they have to drive. Around established transport, predictable permissions should support homes, shops, services, offices, community uses, safe walking and cycling connections, and useful bus interchange, while accommodating necessary vehicle access. Every major station should be a neighbourhood centre, with enough residents and activity nearby to support frequent transport and local life. In greenfield areas, do not repeat the dormitory-suburb model or concentrate every useful destination into one distant activity centre. Government should set clear neighbourhood rules; compliant proposals should have predictable development rights.
policies.system_interaction: Amend the Victorian Planning Provisions and affected schemes while aligning with the Townhouse and Low-Rise Code, small second dwelling rules, Housing Choice and Transport Zone and PSP guidance. Separate two questions that current zoning often bundles together: what compatible uses are permitted, and how much building a location can support. A serviced residential street can permit a broad mix of housing and small local uses while retaining modest height and site-coverage controls; a major station can permit the same broad mix at much greater intensity where transport, utilities and services support it. Map station envelopes when new or upgraded rail is funded; use actual walking access and capacity instead of one uniform radius. Treat major stations as mixed-use neighbourhood centres and coordinate housing permissions with local commerce, services, safe access and public-space planning. In growth areas, require Complete Neighbourhoods sequencing so large residential stages are not released ahead of operational transport and basic local services.
policies.economic_logic: More feasible sites and builders can respond to housing demand; mixed destinations and more residents near transit can support ridership and reduce car dependence. Retaining public land and rental income can return part of publicly created value. These are mechanisms to test against completions, rents, travel behaviour and fiscal outcomes, not a guaranteed saving or universal site return.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Retain fire, structural, disability access, flood, bushfire, contamination, industrial buffer, heritage, canopy and stormwater safeguards, but keep each control tied to the problem it exists to address rather than allowing overlays to quietly recreate blanket exclusionary zoning. Genuine heritage significance should be protected; generic neighbourhood character should not operate as an indefinite veto on otherwise compatible infill housing. Detailed heritage implementation should distinguish significant buildings and precinct values from low-density preservation and be tested before rules are finalised. Protect tenants and public housing through replacement and rights of return. A fixed 20% affordable obligation, 10% free transfer or automatic 50% density bonus is not established for every site. Publish residual-land-value tests and calibrate obligations to uplift; fund public acquisition where an obligation would stop a project. Prevent double-counting of windfall tax, contributions and value capture.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Japanese land-use guidance, OECD research and Victorian planning and infrastructure sources inform this policy. The detailed source corpus will be published through FusionPolicy when available.
policies.implementation_outline: Publish baseline development rights and mapped exclusions; audit utility and service capacity; map real walking catchments around stations; and draft station precinct rules that allow a genuine mix of housing, shops, services and employment rather than housing-only uplift. Prioritise larger envelopes where rail capacity, utilities, schools, open space and safe access can support them. In growth areas, apply Complete Neighbourhoods sequencing so new stations and interchanges become centres from the beginning rather than isolated assets surrounded by later-stage promises.
policies.cost: Site costs and public liabilities need independent modelling
policies.funding: Budgeted investment, public land income and lawful value capture; test debt service and site viability
policies.change_summary: Clarified car-optional station-centred development: make driving a choice, not a prerequisite, while retaining necessary vehicle access.
