policies.title: No Single Points of Failure
policies.summary: Melbourne's rail network has no redundancy: when a single Telstra network fault halted every V/Line train in the state on 8 July 2026, there was no backup for passengers to fall back on. Singapore runs three separate lines through its busiest corridor for exactly this reason. Legislate a redundancy standard for new transit investment, and apply the same principle to bus corridors by pairing route staggering with built-in route overlap.
policies.hook: On 8 July 2026, one Telstra network fault took down every V/Line train in the state at once. Victoria's rail network has no backup route, because nobody designed one in.

key_points.description: On 8 July 2026, a single Telstra network fault halted every V/Line train in Victoria at once. One point of failure in one telco's network stopped the entire regional rail system, because no part of it has an independent fallback.
key_points.point: No backup when V/Line goes down

key_points.description: The East-West Line, Thomson-East Coast Line and Downtown Line all run through Singapore's highest-patronage eastern approach into the CBD. If one line fails, the others still carry passengers.
key_points.point: Singapore builds redundancy into its busiest corridor

key_points.description: Where two or more bus routes already cover the same corridor, staggering them (see Stagger the Timetables) turns overlapping coverage into a high-frequency spine, without needing any single route to independently run turn-up-and-go frequency.
key_points.point: Redundant bus routes let you stagger for free

key_points.description: This mandates that new transit investment be assessed for single points of failure. It directs where the redundancy principle applies rather than committing to a specific, costed build.
key_points.point: A planning standard, not a blank cheque

policies.shareable_quote: One phone company had a bad morning and every V/Line train in the state stopped. That's not bad luck. That's a network with no backup.
policies.design_rationale: Redundancy is standard practice in mature, high-patronage transit networks, because a single line or single dependency failing shouldn't strand an entire corridor. Singapore runs three separate lines, the East-West Line, Thomson-East Coast Line and Downtown Line, through its highest-patronage eastern approach into the CBD for exactly this reason: relief and fallback capacity if any one line has a problem. Victoria's regional rail network has the opposite design. V/Line's entire signalling and communications system depends on a single telco's mobile network, and the 8 July 2026 outage proved that a fault at that single point can halt every train in the state simultaneously. The same principle applies to bus corridors at much lower cost: where two or more routes already cover overlapping ground, that overlap is redundancy that can be actively used, not wasted. Staggering redundant routes, the mechanism specified in Stagger the Timetables, converts route overlap into a de facto high-frequency spine, without requiring any single route to be funded at turn-up-and-go frequency on its own.
policies.system_interaction: V/Line's signalling and train communications currently depend on commercial telco infrastructure with no independent backup, the exact dependency that failed on 8 July 2026. A redundancy standard would require DTP to assess and disclose single points of failure (telco dependency, single-corridor rail alignments, single-operator bus contracts) for major existing and future transit investment. Applying route redundancy to bus corridors interacts directly with the timetable-staggering mechanism in Stagger the Timetables: DTP's existing timetable-setting process would need to treat overlapping routes as a frequency asset to be coordinated, not scheduled independently.
policies.economic_logic: Redundancy has an upfront cost, parallel infrastructure, backup communications systems, but an avoided cost that's easy to underweight until a failure makes it concrete. The 8 July 2026 outage stranded passengers statewide for the duration of the fault, at a cost to commuters and the state's reliability reputation that a backup communications path would have avoided. On buses, the economics are better than on rail: redundant routes are frequently already funded and running, so the only additional cost is the scheduling coordination Stagger the Timetables already specifies, not new capital.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: The main risk is treating this as a one-off response to the July outage rather than a standing planning standard. Without a legislated requirement to assess single points of failure, the same dependency, or an equivalent one, can simply be rebuilt into the network's next generation of infrastructure. On the bus side, coordinating staggered, redundant routes requires the same ongoing DTP compliance discipline as Stagger the Timetables, and carries the same risk of being treated as a one-off audit rather than a standing check.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: The 8 July 2026 Telstra network outage halted every V/Line service in Victoria simultaneously, a documented, dated, statewide failure directly attributable to a single point of failure in train communications infrastructure. Singapore's Thomson-East Coast Line was explicitly built to relieve and provide redundancy for the East-West and North-South Lines on the country's busiest travel corridor, and is being extended to interchange with the Downtown Line, giving that corridor three independent lines. This is an operating, delivered example of the redundancy principle this policy asks Victoria to adopt, not a hypothetical.
policies.implementation_outline: Sequence 1: Legislate a requirement for DTP to assess and publicly disclose single points of failure (telco dependency, single-corridor alignments, single-operator contracts) in current transit infrastructure, starting with the V/Line train communications dependency exposed by the July 2026 outage. Sequence 2: Require new major transit investment business cases to include a redundancy assessment before funding approval. Sequence 3: Direct DTP to identify existing bus corridors with overlapping, redundant routes and apply the Stagger the Timetables mechanism to convert that overlap into coordinated high-frequency spines. Sequence 4: Commission a business case for backup train communications infrastructure independent of a single telco provider.
policies.cost: Audits and backup systems require project-level costing
policies.funding: Cost communications redundancy and route alternatives after identifying failure points. Legislation alone does not deliver backup capacity.

policies.title: Finish the Network
policies.summary: Build the missing rail links as a network, not as isolated projects: electrify overdue growth corridors, create genuinely new orbital coverage in the west, and put stations where they can anchor real neighbourhood centres.
policies.hook: The government's own infrastructure advisor recommended reconfiguring the City Loop years ago. It's still sitting on a shelf while Victoria spends $216 billion on a different rail project entirely.

key_points.description: Finish the long-promised conversion of fast-growing western corridors to metropolitan electric service and reuse existing corridor work wherever it remains fit for purpose.

Use the western orbital leg to connect new catchments through places such as Keilor Village, Watergardens, Caroline Springs, Derrimut, Truganina and Point Cook rather than mostly following existing rail corridors.
key_points.point: Build orbital rail where rail does not exist

key_points.description: Plan new stations with housing, local shops, services, jobs and safe walking access so the railway creates neighbourhoods rather than isolated park-and-ride nodes.
Progress Wallan electrification and City Loop through-running where the case is already substantially developed instead of allowing known network gaps to remain indefinitely.

policies.shareable_quote: Infrastructure Victoria already told them how to fix the City Loop. Nobody funded it. We will.
policies.design_rationale: Melbourne’s problem is not only insufficient capacity on existing lines. Large parts of the outer metropolitan area have no useful rail access at all, while existing and proposed stations are too often treated as isolated transport nodes instead of centres around which housing, shops, services and jobs can cluster. The network therefore needs both more capacity and more coverage. Melton and Wyndham Vale electrification close overdue radial gaps; Wallan should be addressed before the same problem matures further; City Loop reconfiguration extracts more value from existing infrastructure; and a western orbital line should create new rail catchments through currently underserved suburbs rather than largely duplicating corridors that already have rail. New stations on those lines should be planned from the start as mixed-use neighbourhood centres, with tighter spacing where population and urban form justify it.
policies.system_interaction: Melton, Wyndham Vale and Wallan electrification extend the existing metropolitan electrified network and would be delivered through the same Metro Trains/VicTrack operating framework as the rest of the suburban network. City Loop reconfiguration is primarily an operating pattern change requiring signalling and platform allocation work, but it also requires minor new tunnelling to physically connect sections of the loop that are not currently linked for through-running. Most of the infrastructure already exists; completing the loop does not. Cross-platform interchange at Caulfield and Malvern would require platform and track reconfiguration at both stations to align Frankston line and Metro Tunnel/Dandenong corridor services for a same-platform transfer in each direction, in addition to the signalling and platform allocation work already required for City Loop through-running. SRL West is a genuinely new heavy rail corridor and would need to be sequenced against existing Big Build delivery capacity (contractor availability, VicTrack land acquisition processes) rather than delivered in isolation.
policies.economic_logic: The value of new rail is larger when it creates genuinely new access rather than duplicating an existing corridor, and when stations sit inside neighbourhoods that generate trips throughout the day. Capital should therefore be tested against additional population brought within useful rail access, interchange value, service frequency, and the amount of housing and local activity that can be supported within real walking catchments. This does not mean every suburb needs heavy rail or every station needs the same density; it means network coverage and land use should be evaluated together rather than separately.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: A network-coverage objective can still produce poor projects if engineering cost, demand or constructability are ignored. New alignments need real business cases and staged delivery. The opposite risk is allowing business-case processes to become indefinite deferral mechanisms for needs already well established. Station-centre planning can also fail if it becomes a uniform density mandate detached from utilities, schools, open space, accessibility or local conditions. The principle is integrated land use and transport, not identical development everywhere.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: City Loop reconfiguration is Infrastructure Victoria's own Recommendation 60, assessed as producing strong benefits for suburbs on the Craigieburn, Frankston, Upfield and Glen Waverley lines, including relief for northern V/Line services on the Shepparton and Seymour corridors and reliability improvements for the Alamein, Belgrave and Lilydale lines. This is not a novel proposal; it is an existing, costed, government-advised recommendation that has not been actioned. Melton and Wyndham Vale electrification is existing Western Rail Plan (2018) policy. Singapore's City Hall and Raffles Place interchange, where the two adjacent stations between them make every North-South/East-West line transfer a same-platform walk rather than a stairs-and-corridor trip, is a well-established precedent for minimising transfer friction between two intersecting metro lines without requiring a single mega-interchange station to handle every transfer direction. The general principle of directing capital toward underserved corridors ahead of duplicating existing ones follows the same logic applied internationally wherever transit investment prioritises network coverage over redundant capacity.
policies.implementation_outline: Sequence 1: Move Melton and Wyndham Vale electrification from repeated planning into funded delivery, reusing existing corridor investigations and future-proofing where fit for purpose. Sequence 2: Update and progress the City Loop through-running work and commit Wallan electrification to the medium-term pipeline. Sequence 3: Develop the western orbital alignment around the objective of creating new rail catchments—Airport to Watergardens via Keilor Village, then through western growth suburbs toward Point Cook—rather than treating completion of a branded loop as the objective in itself. Sequence 4: For every new station, jointly plan rail access, local street connections, housing capacity, compatible commerce and services so stations open as neighbourhood centres rather than transport islands.
policies.cost: Each corridor and network change needs a staged business case
policies.funding: Publish route, capacity, capital and operating appraisals before selecting projects and funding sources.
policies.change_summary: Clarified the network philosophy: western rail should create genuinely new catchments, and new stations should be planned as mixed-use neighbourhood centres rather than isolated transport nodes.

policies.title: End FlexiRide's Fake Flexibility
policies.summary: FlexiRide and similar on-demand services currently require hours of lead time and can still drop passengers hundreds of metres short of their actual destination. Legislate minimum service standards for on-demand transit: maximum booking lead time, and door-to-door rather than zone-to-zone delivery.
policies.hook: A FlexiRide booking near Woodgrove needed three hours' notice for a fifteen-minute ride, and still dropped the passenger 800 metres short of their front door.

key_points.description: A Woodgrove-area FlexiRide booking required three hours' notice for a fifteen-minute ride, and still dropped the passenger 800m short of their destination, on a trip that would otherwise be a 7.3km, roughly 100-minute walk.
key_points.point: Three hours for a fifteen-minute ride

key_points.description: On-demand services that drop passengers short of their actual destination shift the last leg of the trip back onto the passenger, defeating the point of booking a ride.
This legislates minimums for an existing service model, no new vehicles or routes required.
key_points.point: A service standard, not new infrastructure

policies.shareable_quote: Three hours' notice for a fifteen-minute ride that still leaves you 800 metres from your own door isn't on-demand. It's slower and less reliable than the walk it was supposed to replace.
policies.design_rationale: Rather than replacing on-demand services, this legislates the minimum standards that make 'on-demand' an honest label: a maximum booking lead time, and door-to-door rather than zone-to-zone delivery. This preserves the flexibility of the on-demand model for genuinely low-density areas while removing the specific failure modes that currently make it worse than no service at all.
policies.system_interaction: On-demand services like FlexiRide are contracted and specified by DTP; this legislates binding minimum standards into those service specifications and future contracts, rather than requiring new vehicles, routes, or booking infrastructure.
policies.economic_logic: This is a service standard applied to already-funded contracts, not a new spending commitment. The fix is to what these services are contractually required to deliver, not how much is spent delivering them.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Operators may argue that tighter lead-time and door-to-door requirements increase per-trip cost or reduce the number of trips a given fleet can service; this needs to be weighed against the current failure mode, where excessive lead times and zone drop-offs mean the service isn't being used at all in the situations it was meant to solve.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: On-demand transit services overseas that succeed at replacing fixed-route low-frequency services typically guarantee short booking windows (well under an hour) and true door-to-door delivery; FlexiRide's current lead times and zone-based drop-offs fall well outside that benchmark.
policies.implementation_outline: Sequence 1: Legislate a maximum booking lead time for on-demand transit services. Sequence 2: Legislate a door-to-door delivery requirement, replacing zone-to-zone drop-offs. Sequence 3: Apply the new standards to FlexiRide and equivalent services at next contract renewal.
policies.cost: Service, dispatch and contract changes require costing
policies.funding: Test the standard at contract renewal and fund any added driver hours, vehicles or dispatch support.

policies.title: Fix the Order, Not Just the Fare
policies.summary: Improve coverage, frequency and reliability before considering fare-free travel. Publish the service and fare trade-offs.
policies.hook: Free public transport sounds bold until you realise it does nothing for the Melton resident who has no service to board in the first place.

key_points.description: VAGO found only 9-12% of Melton's population within reach of high-quality public transport. A fare cut does nothing for someone with no service to board.
VAGO also found only 68-73% of priority bus-to-train connections fall within a workable 5-10 minute window. A free fare on an unreliable connection does not fix the connection.
Free-fares-first policy spends political capital on the cheapest thing to change, leaving the actual constraints, coverage and reliability, untouched.
key_points.point: Fare is the easy variable, not the broken one

policies.shareable_quote: A free ticket for a bus that never comes isn't a policy. Fix the order: coverage, then frequency, then fare.
policies.design_rationale: This is a sequencing stance, not a rejection of free fares as an eventual goal. The three-step hierarchy (coverage, then frequency and reliability, then fare) reflects which constraint actually stops people using public transport today. Legislating fare policy ahead of the other two risks locking in a popular but premature commitment that does not move ridership, because people without a usable service or a reliable connection do not benefit from a lower price.
policies.system_interaction: This staging commitment would bind future fare legislation to prior benchmarks on coverage (the one-kilometre standard) and reliability (priority connection windows), both independently measurable through DTP and VAGO reporting mechanisms already in use elsewhere in this platform.
policies.economic_logic: Patronage economics improve as coverage and reliability improve: more usable, more reliable services generate more fare revenue and more political room to reduce fares sustainably. Cutting fares first, before patronage has grown, means the same revenue shortfall has to be met from general revenue instead of being offset by increased ridership, making the fare cut harder to sustain long-term.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: The risk is being cast as opposing free transport rather than sequencing it correctly; the staging framing needs to be maintained consistently to avoid this being conflated with opposition to the Greens' destination, which Fusion shares.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: VAGO's June 2026 Bus Plan audit is the source for both the coverage figure (9-12% of Melton within reach of high-quality PT) and the reliability figure (68-73% of priority bus-to-train connections within a 5-10 minute window) underpinning this staging argument.
policies.implementation_outline: Sequence 1: Formalise the three-step staging commitment (coverage, frequency/reliability, fare) as a public position ahead of any fare legislation. Sequence 2: Tie future fare policy debate to published coverage and reliability benchmarks rather than allowing it to proceed independently. Sequence 3: Support fare reform once coverage and reliability benchmarks are substantially met.
policies.cost: Sequencing position; service upgrades and any fare change need separate costings
policies.funding: Cost coverage and frequency improvements before fare reform. No automatic fare reduction or saving is assumed.

policies.title: Connect the Regions
policies.summary: Victoria's regional network is built entirely hub-and-spoke through Melbourne. A Ballarat resident travelling to Bendigo has to route via the city despite the two being roughly 100km apart directly. Commission a direct regional cross-connectivity study for major regional-to-regional pairs currently requiring a Melbourne detour.
policies.hook: Want to get from Ballarat to Bendigo, two of Victoria's biggest regional cities about 100km apart, without a car? The only way DTP has built is via Melbourne.

key_points.description: Every V/Line and coach route is designed around getting people to and from Melbourne, not between regional centres.
key_points.point: Regional Victoria isn't a Melbourne feeder

key_points.description: Two of Victoria's largest regional cities, roughly 100km apart directly, have no direct public transport connection at all.
key_points.point: Ballarat to Bendigo, the test case

key_points.description: This is a commitment to find out what direct regional links would cost and where they'd have the most impact, not a pre-committed spend.
key_points.point: A scoping study, not a blank cheque

policies.shareable_quote: Regional Victoria isn't a feeder system for Melbourne. It's time the network stopped treating it like one.
policies.design_rationale: A scoping study is the deliverable this term rather than a funded build, because the specific cost and alignment of direct regional-to-regional services isn't known. DTP has never studied it, because the network was never designed around that question. Naming a study rather than a project avoids overpromising on figures that don't exist yet, while still forcing the question onto the public record.
policies.system_interaction: V/Line operates the regional rail network and coach replacement services under its existing franchise arrangements; any new direct regional-to-regional service would need to interact with existing rolling stock allocation, track access agreements (much of regional track is shared with freight), and V/Line timetabling systems.
policies.economic_logic: Hub-and-spoke design made sense when Melbourne was the overwhelming destination for regional travel; as regional centres grow in their own right, demand for direct regional-to-regional travel grows independent of Melbourne, and the current network structurally cannot serve it without a Melbourne detour that adds hours to trips a direct link could complete quickly.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: The primary risk is that a scoping study is commissioned and then shelved without a funding pathway. That's the same failure mode already seen with Infrastructure Victoria's City Loop recommendation. A firm reporting deadline and public release requirement should be attached to the study commission to reduce this risk.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Infrastructure Victoria and V/Line planning documents to date have focused overwhelmingly on Melbourne-radial services; no equivalent regional cross-connectivity study currently exists for Victoria, despite comparable regional rail systems overseas demonstrating demand for non-hub regional links where population centres are large enough to support them.
policies.implementation_outline: Sequence 1: Commission a direct regional cross-connectivity study covering major regional-to-regional pairs currently requiring a Melbourne detour, starting with Ballarat–Bendigo. Sequence 2: Require the study to assess both V/Line rail and coach options against cost and demand. Sequence 3: Publish the findings and recommended priority order publicly, with a fixed reporting deadline.
policies.cost: TBD. Needs a scoping study.
policies.funding: The study itself is a modest departmental commissioning cost; any resulting service build would be costed and funded separately once the study reports, not committed to in advance.

policies.title: Set a Transit Access Standard
policies.summary: Set and publish a statewide public-transport access standard based on real walking distance, service frequency and span—not a nominal stop within an arbitrary radius.
policies.hook: A bus stop is not transport access if you cannot safely reach it or the bus barely runs.

key_points.description: Assess access using the real walking network, safe crossings, service frequency and operating span rather than straight-line distance to any stop.
Set appropriate minimum access expectations for metropolitan growth areas, established suburbs, regional centres and genuinely rural communities instead of pretending one distance rule fits all.
DTP publishes an annual map showing where residents fail the access standard and the funded program for closing the highest-impact gaps.

policies.shareable_quote: Don't count bus stops. Count whether people can actually use the network.
policies.design_rationale: A nearby bus stop is not useful public transport if the route runs too rarely, finishes before people can get home, sits across an unsafe arterial or requires an impractical walking route. Later Fusion transport work therefore treats accessibility as a service-and-network problem rather than a radius on a map. A statewide standard should make those dimensions measurable while recognising that the appropriate floor differs between dense metropolitan areas, growth suburbs, regional towns and rural Victoria.
policies.system_interaction: Require DTP to publish a statewide transit-access methodology and annual compliance map using network walking distance, safe pedestrian access, frequency and service span. Set transparent place-based minimums through regulation after public modelling. Use the results to prioritise bus-network reform, new stops, pedestrian links and other gap-closing investment alongside the Complete Neighbourhoods and Transit Deserts programs.
policies.economic_logic: A nominal coverage target can be met cheaply by adding infrequent routes that few people can use, creating the appearance of access without meaningful mobility. Measuring useful access directs operating and capital spending toward interventions that actually expand people's reachable jobs, services and education.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: An overly rigid statewide metric can misallocate service in low-density areas, while a weak metric can be gamed with token services. Publish the methodology and raw indicators, distinguish geographic contexts, measure both coverage and service quality, and review thresholds against observed patronage and accessibility outcomes.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: This mirrors the logic of the existing Transport Score tool (transportscore.fusionparty.org.au), which already measures and publishes transit access at a suburb level; this policy legislates a minimum floor against that same measurement rather than leaving access purely descriptive.
policies.implementation_outline: Publish the baseline first. DTP should map real walking access, frequency and span across Victoria, identify the largest population and disadvantage-weighted gaps, consult on place-based minimum standards, then attach funded gap-closing programs and annual reporting.
policies.cost: Mapping, service coverage and ongoing operations require costing
policies.funding: Use a costed transit program; proposed parking and land revenue cannot be booked before rates and receipts are tested.

policies.title: Stagger the Timetables
policies.summary: Where two bus routes share a corridor, DTP frequently schedules them to arrive at the same time instead of staggered, halving effective frequency for free. Mandate a statewide audit and correction of every shared-corridor timetable clash.
policies.hook: DTP is running two buses on the same corridor at the same time and calling it two services. Melton commuters get the frequency of one.

key_points.description: Staggering two routes that already run the same corridor turns two simultaneous 40-minute services into one effective 20-minute corridor, no new buses required.
Melton's 457 and 459 are the clearest example, but DTP has never audited how many other shared corridors have the same clash.
This is a scheduling correction, not a service increase, deliverable by ministerial direction without a budget line.

policies.shareable_quote: Two buses on one corridor, running on the same clock. Stagger them and you've doubled the service for free.
policies.design_rationale: A mandated audit is chosen over a service-by-service fix because the Melton case is unlikely to be the only instance. Wherever two routes share a corridor for even part of their length, unstaggered timetables silently halve the effective frequency residents experience. It costs nothing to correct once identified, but nobody is currently checking for it.
policies.system_interaction: DTP already sets and publishes timetables for every metropolitan and regional bus route; this requires no new systems, only a cross-referencing audit of shared-corridor timing across the existing timetable dataset, followed by rescheduling directives issued through the same process DTP already uses to publish timetable changes.
policies.economic_logic: Because the buses, drivers, and routes are already funded, staggering is a pure efficiency gain: the same operating budget delivers double the effective frequency on affected corridors. It is the cheapest frequency improvement available anywhere in the network, because it requires no new expenditure at all.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: The main risk is that DTP treats the audit as a one-off exercise rather than an ongoing check. Timetables change regularly, and a new clash can be introduced at the next reschedule just as easily as an old one is fixed. The audit and correction process should be a standing compliance check, not a single pass.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Pulse or clockface scheduling, deliberately staggering services that share a corridor so combined frequency is even rather than bunched, is standard practice in mature transit networks internationally. Melton's 457/459 pairing is a documented case where this basic principle was not applied despite both routes being run by DTP-contracted operators on published timetables.
policies.implementation_outline: Sequence 1: Mandate a DTP audit of every shared-corridor pairing statewide, cross-referencing published timetables for services that overlap in time on shared sections. Sequence 2: Publish the audit findings, including every clash identified. Sequence 3: Issue rescheduling directives to correct each clash. Sequence 4: Make the audit a standing annual compliance check, not a one-off.
policies.cost: Timetable audit and changes need operational assessment
policies.funding: Use DTP planning capacity, then cost any fleet, driver or connection changes identified by the audit.

policies.title: Nothing Without the People
policies.summary: Create a safeguarded citizen-initiative process for major democratic and constitutional questions, beginning with deliberation and advisory votes rather than an unrestricted popular veto over ordinary legislation.
policies.hook: Voting every four years should not be the only way Victorians can force a major democratic question onto Parliament’s agenda.

key_points.description: A substantial, geographically distributed petition can trigger independent review and a representative deliberative process on an eligible statewide question.
Questions must satisfy constitutional, human-rights, anti-discrimination and electoral-integrity requirements and cannot be used to target individuals or strip protected minorities of equal rights.
Eligible initiatives can proceed to an advisory statewide vote that Parliament must debate and formally respond to; constitutional changes continue through the lawful constitutional process.

policies.shareable_quote: Give people a way to put major questions on the ballot—without turning rights or complex law into a petition contest.
policies.design_rationale: People should have a route to place major democratic questions on the public agenda between elections, but a raw signature threshold followed by a binding yes/no vote can amplify money, misinformation and majority power over minority rights. A safer model combines a demanding and geographically broad petition threshold with independent legal review, representative deliberation, transparent campaign finance and an advisory public vote that Parliament cannot ignore. Binding constitutional change should occur only through the constitutional process that lawfully applies to it.
policies.system_interaction: Create an ordinary-legislation citizen initiative process. A qualifying petition must meet both a statewide signature threshold and geographic-distribution requirements. An independent body verifies signatures and tests whether the question is legally eligible and compatible with protected rights. A stratified citizens’ panel then examines the proposal and publishes recommendations before an advisory statewide vote. Parliament must debate the result and issue a recorded response within a fixed period. The mechanism cannot directly repeal ordinary legislation, appropriate money, decide individual cases or bypass constitutional requirements.
policies.economic_logic: Citizen initiative can force neglected issues onto the agenda and create political accountability between elections. Advisory rather than automatic binding effect preserves the information value of a statewide vote without creating abrupt policy instability or allowing well-funded campaigns to rewrite complex law through a single binary question. Geographic thresholds, spending transparency and deliberation increase the cost of manufactured campaigns while preserving a route for genuinely broad public movements.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Initiative systems can be captured by wealthy campaigners, weaponised against minorities, flooded with simplistic questions or used so frequently that participation collapses. Safeguards should include geographic signature requirements, strict donation and expenditure transparency, neutral question testing, rights review, a deliberative stage, limits on repeat questions and a clear list of matters unsuitable for direct initiative. The mechanism should be independently reviewed after initial use before any proposal to make outcomes binding.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Switzerland holds federal referenda three to four times per year on average, with turnout ranging from roughly 40% to over 70% depending on the question. The Swiss Federal Chancellery publishes full results and campaign spending for each referendum. Ireland's 2018 abortion referendum, produced by a Citizens' Assembly recommendation, is the most recent example of a deliberative-then-referendum process producing a clear democratic mandate for significant constitutional change: 66.4% voted in favour of repealing the Eighth Amendment. New Zealand's non-binding citizens-initiated referenda, available under the Citizens Initiated Referenda Act 1993, have been used on matters including election law and retirement savings policy, with governments not legally bound by results but politically affected by strong majorities.
policies.implementation_outline: Legislate an advisory citizen-initiative framework and independent eligibility process, model petition and geographic thresholds publicly, establish campaign-finance and question-integrity rules, and evaluate the first several initiatives before considering any expansion. Constitutional amendments remain subject to the Constitution Act and any applicable entrenchment requirements.
policies.cost: Referendum design and administration require costing
policies.funding: Fund electoral administration and accessibility after the legal model is settled.

policies.title: Communities Set Policy
policies.summary: Give communities direct control over a defined share of discretionary local public investment through participatory budgeting—without creating a local veto over housing, land use or statewide infrastructure.
policies.hook: People should have a real say over the local public improvements their taxes fund—not a veto over who else gets to live nearby.

key_points.description: Residents vote on a defined pool of discretionary local capital spending for public spaces, walking and cycling links, community facilities, local environmental works and similar improvements.
Participatory budgeting cannot block compliant housing, override statewide planning rules or housing targets, or give existing residents a veto over who may live in a neighbourhood.
Use transparent eligibility rules, deliberative panels and participation safeguards so organised minorities cannot capture low-turnout local votes.

policies.shareable_quote: Give communities a budget and a vote—not a veto over their future neighbours.
policies.design_rationale: Participatory budgeting is useful when it gives residents meaningful control over discretionary public investment. It becomes counterproductive when 'community control' is confused with control over development rights. Victoria needs both stronger democratic participation and a housing system in which compatible homes, shops and services can proceed under clear statewide rules. Existing residents should be able to help choose local public improvements, but should not gain an exclusionary veto over new residents or otherwise compliant housing.
policies.system_interaction: Create a state-funded participatory budgeting allocation administered locally under statewide rules. Eligible categories should be limited to discretionary public capital improvements such as public space, active-transport links, community facilities, local environmental works and small accessibility or amenity projects. Explicitly exclude statutory planning decisions, development approvals, rezoning vetoes, housing targets, essential network infrastructure and recurrent services. Projects remain subject to normal law, technical standards and rights protections.
policies.economic_logic: A bounded participatory budget can reveal locally valuable small projects that central capital programs overlook while preserving network-wide planning and housing supply. Keeping land-use entitlements and essential infrastructure outside the mechanism prevents incumbent residents from imposing exclusionary costs on future residents or blocking projects whose benefits extend beyond one neighbourhood.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Local participation can be captured by organised, higher-turnout groups and can become a vehicle for exclusion if its remit is vague. The safeguard is structural: define the spending pool and eligible project classes in law; exclude housing and development vetoes; use representative deliberative panels before public voting where appropriate; publish participation and distribution data; and review whether funding reaches underserved communities.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Paris's participatory budgeting program allocated EUR 100 million in city capital spending in 2014, with 77,000 participants voting on projects submitted by residents. By subsequent cycles, participation had grown to over 100,000 voters. Porto Alegre's program (1989 to mid-2000s) is the most-studied example in the academic literature, with documented effects including an increase in the share of the capital budget reaching lower-income neighbourhoods, improved sewerage coverage, and higher school enrolment rates in areas where participatory budgeting allocated infrastructure funding. Scottish Government's participatory budgeting program, legislated in 2021, requires each Scottish council to run at least one participatory budgeting process annually, with a state-funded pot of at least 1% of the devolved budget available for community allocation: this is the closest direct legislative precedent for what this policy proposes.
policies.implementation_outline: Pilot a defined participatory capital fund in several contrasting Victorian communities. Set eligible project categories and explicit exclusions in advance, use transparent nomination and voting rules with representative deliberation where needed, publish results and participation data, and evaluate distributional outcomes before scaling.
policies.cost: Community boards and participatory budgeting require administration and accessibility funding
policies.funding: Set a transparent allocation from existing planning and development budgets, with any new cost appropriated.

policies.title: Citizens in Every Room
policies.summary: Use representative citizens’ panels for major, genuinely contested long-term questions to improve deliberation and scrutiny—without creating a parallel legislature or another veto point for routine housing and infrastructure delivery.
policies.hook: Public consultation should mean more than collecting submissions after the important choices have already been made.

key_points.description: Convene stratified citizens’ panels for selected major long-term or institutionally difficult questions, not every Bill or routine administrative decision.
Give participants balanced evidence, competing expert views and enough time to deliberate, with transparent rules for question design and facilitation.
Panels make public recommendations and Parliament or government must formally respond; elected institutions remain responsible for the final decision unless a separate lawful referendum is required.

policies.shareable_quote: Put ordinary Victorians in the room for the hard questions—and make government answer them.
policies.design_rationale: Sortition can bring people who are not lobbyists, party officials or habitual consultation participants into difficult public decisions. Its value is deliberative: a representative group can examine evidence, trade-offs and competing interests in depth. That does not justify inserting a citizens’ panel into every Bill, planning permit or infrastructure approval. Used selectively, panels can improve legitimacy and expose blind spots without becoming a parallel legislature or an additional mechanism for delaying routine delivery.
policies.system_interaction: Establish a statutory framework allowing Parliament or government to convene stratified citizens’ panels for defined major questions. The remit, selection method, evidence process, funding and conflicts must be public. Recommendations are published and require a formal government or parliamentary response within a set period. Panels do not replace Parliament, courts, independent regulators or ordinary by-right planning rules, and are not required for routine development approvals or delivery of infrastructure already authorised under general law.
policies.economic_logic: Well-designed deliberation can reduce the cost of poorly framed major reforms by exposing trade-offs before positions harden. But mandatory deliberation on routine decisions would itself create delay and transaction costs. A selective model concentrates the process where uncertainty, distributional conflict or long-term institutional consequences justify the additional time.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Panels can be manipulated through question framing, participant selection, facilitator bias or selective evidence, and can be misused to launder a decision already made. They can also become a new veto or delay mechanism if applied indiscriminately. Require independent stratified selection, balanced evidence, publication of materials and dissent, transparent funding and facilitation, and a tightly defined remit. Recommendations should inform accountable decision-makers rather than silently displace them.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Ireland's Citizens' Assembly (2016-18) was established by Dail resolution with 99 members, one randomly selected chairperson and 98 randomly selected citizens stratified by age, gender, and regional distribution. It produced recommendations on abortion law reform that led directly to the 2018 referendum in which 66.4% voted to repeal the Eighth Amendment. The same assembly produced recommendations on climate action, fixed-term parliaments, and ageing, all of which resulted in policy or legislative responses. Paris's participatory budgeting program allocated EUR 100 million in city capital spending to projects chosen by residents voting directly through a digital platform, with 77,000 participants in 2014 growing to over 100,000 in subsequent cycles. Porto Alegre's participatory budgeting, which ran from 1989 to the mid-2000s, allocated up to 21% of the municipal budget through neighbourhood assemblies and distributed elected delegates, producing documented improvements in sewerage, road paving, and schools in lower-income areas.
policies.implementation_outline: Legislate a common integrity framework for citizens’ panels and pilot it on a small number of major statewide questions. Publish selection methodology, evidence, recommendations, minority views and the formal government response. Independently evaluate representativeness and influence before expanding use.
policies.cost: Assembly recruitment, accessibility, facilitation and reporting require funding
policies.funding: Fund citizen assemblies through an explicit public appropriation, with scope and cost published before rollout.

policies.title: Expose Hidden Campaign Labour
policies.summary: Require parties and candidates to disclose material paid, seconded and professionally supplied campaign labour that would otherwise hide outside ordinary donation reporting—without forcing genuine grassroots volunteers to keep political timesheets.
policies.hook: A campaign should not be able to hide a professional operation simply because the support arrived as staff time instead of cash.

key_points.description: Disclose material campaign work supplied by companies, unions, advocacy organisations or other entities when the worker is paid or directed by that entity.
Do not require ordinary unpaid members and supporters volunteering in their personal capacity to log every hour with the electoral regulator.
Use clear valuation and disclosure rules for professional services, staff secondments, data, logistics and other material non-cash campaign support.

policies.shareable_quote: Track the hidden professional support. Leave genuine volunteers free to volunteer.
policies.design_rationale: Transparency rules should reveal organised resources supplied to campaigns without turning ordinary political participation into regulated labour. A staff member seconded by an employer, a professional service donated by a firm, or a coordinated external campaign operation can carry substantial economic value and potential influence. That is different from a supporter knocking on doors after work. Disclosure should follow the material resource and the organisation supplying it, not burden genuine volunteers with timesheets.
policies.system_interaction: Amend Victorian electoral disclosure rules so material paid or employer-directed campaign labour and professional in-kind services are valued and disclosed consistently with other non-cash political support. Define de minimis thresholds and a clear exemption for genuine unpaid personal volunteering. The VEC should publish guidance distinguishing personal volunteer activity from labour or services supplied by an organisation. Public-election-funding thresholds should be considered separately on their own merits rather than bundled into this disclosure policy.
policies.economic_logic: Non-cash professional support can substitute directly for campaign expenditure. Transparent valuation prevents organisations from avoiding donation rules by supplying labour or services instead of money, while exempting genuine volunteering avoids compliance costs that would disproportionately hurt small parties and community campaigns.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Overbroad rules could deter volunteering and impose large compliance costs on small campaigns; weak rules could allow paid or directed labour to be relabelled as volunteering. Use materiality thresholds, focus on organisationally supplied resources, exempt genuine personal volunteering, and require disclosure of the supplying entity rather than surveillance of individual volunteers.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Victoria currently requires a candidate to receive at least 4% of first-preference votes or be elected before public election funding is available. Victorian Government electoral-review material has identified that electorate-by-electorate thresholds can disadvantage minor parties relative to their statewide support. The Centre for Public Integrity proposed reducing the threshold to 2% with a bona-fide-candidacy safeguard, while another submission to Victoria's independent electoral review proposed a 0% public-funding threshold. Fusion Victoria's preferred model is no vote-share threshold, while retaining nomination, registration, expenditure, audit and compliance safeguards.
policies.implementation_outline: Ask the VEC to model existing treatment of secondments and professional in-kind support, define materiality and personal-volunteer exemptions, then legislate consistent valuation and disclosure rules with proportionate penalties for deliberate concealment.
policies.cost: Disclosure systems, audit and enforcement require funding
policies.funding: Model the additional public-funding cost using VEC election returns before commencement. Payments remain reimbursement-limited: removing the threshold extends eligibility to genuine electoral expenditure associated with votes currently excluded from the funding formula; it does not create an unrestricted cash payment per vote.

policies.title: End Cash-for-Access Politics
policies.summary: End political fundraising models that sell private access to ministers, MPs or candidates. Require paid political-access events and material policy discussions to be transparent, while preserving ordinary fundraising and open engagement with businesses, unions, community groups and citizens.
policies.hook: Everyone should be able to make their case to government. Nobody should be able to buy a private door into it.

key_points.description: Political donations or expensive tickets must not purchase exclusive private access to ministers, MPs or candidates.
Disclose material ticket purchases, sponsors, attendees receiving political access and the nature of organised policy-engagement events under clear thresholds.
Businesses, unions, charities, experts and community organisations can still meet representatives and contribute to public debate; money should not determine who gets privileged private access.

policies.shareable_quote: Hear from business. Hear from unions. Hear from communities. Just don't sell the private meeting.
policies.design_rationale: The integrity problem is not that a corporation, union or community organisation speaks to an elected representative. Representatives should hear from affected groups. The problem is a market in access: paying a large fundraising price buys private proximity to decision-makers unavailable to ordinary citizens, with little visibility of what was discussed. Regulation should target the financial privilege and secrecy rather than treating participation by particular classes of organisation as inherently illegitimate.
policies.system_interaction: Amend electoral and integrity rules to define paid political-access events, require timely disclosure of material ticket purchases and sponsorship, and prohibit fundraising arrangements in which payment purchases exclusive private access to an office-holder or candidate. Coordinate this with ministerial diary, lobbying and donation disclosure so the public can see both the financial relationship and significant policy access. Ordinary community events, membership fundraising and non-exclusive stakeholder meetings remain lawful.
policies.economic_logic: Transparent, non-exclusive access reduces the risk that policy is shaped by whoever can pay the highest entry price while preserving useful information exchange between government and affected sectors. Targeting the transaction is also less distortionary than banning broad categories of organisations from political participation.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Poor drafting could capture ordinary fundraising dinners, community events or legitimate stakeholder engagement, while narrow drafting could simply move paid access into sponsorships or bundled packages. Define the prohibited benefit around exclusive access purchased through financial contribution, use materiality thresholds, aggregate low-value ordinary attendance where appropriate, and align disclosure across donations, lobbying and ministerial diaries.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: The Irish Electoral Reform Act 2022 introduced stricter donation disclosure requirements and caps on third-party spending, building on an existing culture of relatively low disclosure thresholds. Switzerland's federal ban on anonymous donations above CHF 100 (approximately AUD 170) and mandatory public disclosure of all party funding sources above CHF 10,000 per donor per year has produced a more transparent public record of which corporate interests fund which parties. Victoria's own 2023 property developer donation ban establishes the precedent that category-specific bans are constitutional and administratively workable under state electoral law.
policies.implementation_outline: Legislate a paid-access disclosure category and prohibit sale of exclusive private political access; align reporting with donation and ministerial-diary systems; publish guidance for ordinary fundraising and stakeholder engagement; and review avoidance patterns after the first election cycle.
policies.cost: Legislation, disclosure and enforcement costs to be assessed
policies.funding: Budget for electoral oversight and enforcement; do not assume compliance is free.

policies.title: Expose Preference Deal Money
policies.summary: Victoria abolished group voting tickets for Legislative Council elections in August 2026. Voters now direct at least five preferences above or below the line. Disclose any money or in-kind support tied to preference recommendations and how-to-vote deals.
policies.hook: Victoria ended upper-house group voting tickets. The next test is whether voters can see the money behind political preference recommendations.

key_points.description: At least five choices above or below the line under the 2026 reform.
Group voting tickets no longer apply to Victorian Legislative Council elections.
Test a narrow, enforceable rule for consideration tied to how-to-vote recommendations.

policies.shareable_quote: Victoria scrapped group voting tickets. Good. Now make the money behind preference recommendations visible.
policies.design_rationale: The Electoral Amendment (Miscellaneous Matters) Act 2026 removed group voting tickets from Victorian Legislative Council elections in August. Voters must number at least five boxes above or below the line. This policy's original abolition ask has been achieved; its remaining transparency proposal concerns any consideration attached to how-to-vote recommendations. Group voting tickets still apply in Melbourne City Council elections, a separate jurisdictional question.
policies.system_interaction: Update political finance and how-to-vote disclosure rules, subject to legal drafting, so parties and campaigners disclose relevant paid or in-kind preference recommendation arrangements. Existing donation, expenditure and authorisation rules must be reconciled; no claim is made that all such deals currently evade disclosure. Preserve voter choice under the new upper-house ballot.
policies.economic_logic: The GVT abolition removes automatic party-directed preference transfers in state upper-house elections. Disclosure of paid recommendation arrangements can help voters assess campaign advocacy; the scope, enforcement cost and interaction with existing finance law need legal review.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: Avoid falsely equating an ordinary published how-to-vote recommendation with a purchased vote. Define reportable consideration, timing, valuation and enforcement proportionately, while protecting legitimate association and speech.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: Victorian Electoral Commission, 2026 Electoral Act amendments and preferential voting: https://www.vec.vic.gov.au/about-us/legislation/electoral-act-amendments-2026 ; https://www.vec.vic.gov.au/voting/how-voting-works/preferential-voting
policies.implementation_outline: Acknowledge the August 2026 reform as achieved. Review the new Act, VEC guidance and existing finance disclosures; draft a narrow disclosure amendment for consideration linked to how-to-vote recommendations and publish the remaining gaps.

policies.title: Fund the Outer Suburbs
policies.summary: Create a transparent growth-area infrastructure program that directs transport and local infrastructure funding to documented service gaps, population growth and project value—not an arbitrary geographic quota.
policies.hook: New suburbs should not spend their first twenty years waiting for the infrastructure that should have arrived with the houses.

key_points.description: Use published measures of population growth, access, service deficits, disadvantage and project benefits to prioritise investment in fast-growing and underserved communities.
Sequence buses, schools, walking links, drainage, community facilities and other essential infrastructure with growth instead of years after residents move in.
Report where metropolitan infrastructure money goes, the service gap each project addresses and why it ranked above alternatives.

policies.shareable_quote: Build the infrastructure with the suburb—not a generation after it.
policies.design_rationale: Growth areas repeatedly receive housing before the transport, schools, walking networks and local services needed to make those communities work. The correction should be structural, but a fixed percentage of the entire major-project budget is too blunt: needs and project value change over time, and worthwhile projects should not become unfundable because they sit on the wrong side of a geographic quota. A published needs-and-benefits framework can give growth-area deficits proper weight while preserving network-wide planning.
policies.system_interaction: Require the state infrastructure and budget process to publish metropolitan allocations and assess growth-area projects against consistent measures including population growth, transport accessibility, infrastructure backlog, disadvantage, housing delivery and whole-of-network benefits. Establish a dedicated growth-area program for projects that are routinely too small or cross-portfolio to compete with megaprojects, while leaving major network investments subject to transparent statewide assessment.
policies.economic_logic: Infrastructure delivered alongside growth avoids the household costs and productivity losses created when new suburbs are designed around compulsory car ownership and long trips to basic services. Transparent prioritisation directs capital toward high-value deficits without assuming that every dollar spent outside growth areas is wasteful or that a fixed geographic share will remain economically justified.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: A growth-area program can become another political grants pool, while a rigid formula can fund weak projects simply to satisfy a quota. Publish criteria, project rankings and post-completion outcomes; require benefits to be assessed at network and community level; prevent ministers from substituting low-value local announcements for essential strategic infrastructure; and periodically update the weighting as population and service gaps change.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: The Mental Health and Wellbeing Levy, in force since 1 January 2022, adds 0.5% on payrolls above $10 million and an additional 0.5% above $100 million, with revenue ring-fenced by statute for mental health services: this is the entire Versement Mobilite mechanism applied to a different purpose, demonstrating it is administratively and constitutionally workable in Victoria. The French Versement Mobilite has operated since 1971 and is the largest single revenue source for most French metropolitan transit networks. Scotland's Transport (Scotland) Act 2019 gave regional transport partnerships the power to levy workplace parking charges and cordon road user charges, with revenue hypothecated to local transport investment: this is the same principle applied to parking rather than payroll.
policies.implementation_outline: Publish a metropolitan infrastructure baseline showing population growth, accessibility and service gaps; establish a dedicated cross-portfolio growth-area program with transparent assessment criteria; require infrastructure sequencing plans for major new growth; and report annual allocations and delivery against the baseline.
policies.cost: Budget reallocation has an opportunity cost; projects need appraisal
policies.funding: Test any reallocation against projects displaced, existing growth-area charges and legal limits before assigning revenue.

supporting_research.title: Woodgrove and Melton: Why Transit Sequencing Matters Before Parking Reduction

policies.title: Fix Transit Deserts
policies.summary: Build a high-frequency outer-suburban bus grid now, while planning rail and activity centres so fast-growing suburbs are not permanently locked into car dependence.
policies.hook: We don't care if you want to drive. We care if you have to drive.

key_points.description: Run frequent orbital and cross-suburban routes so neighbouring suburbs can connect without travelling through the CBD.
Measure frequency, span and real walking access—not just whether a bus stop exists somewhere nearby.
Design routes around real destinations and interchanges, with stations functioning as mixed-use neighbourhood centres rather than isolated endpoints.

policies.shareable_quote: You don't need a light rail study. You need a bus every 10 minutes. We'll build that first, with dedicated lanes so it actually runs on time.
policies.design_rationale: The immediate gap is bus service, but the deeper problem is a network and land-use pattern that leaves too many outer-suburban residents far from any useful transport or local destination. High-frequency buses are the fastest way to give existing suburbs practical alternatives to driving, while future rail investment should create additional station catchments and mixed-use centres instead of relying on a small number of distant activity centres. Buses, rail and land use should be treated as one accessibility system: feeder routes must reach stations, orbital routes must connect neighbouring suburbs directly, and stations should sit inside places people can actually walk to and use.
policies.system_interaction: The Bus Plan was announced in 2021 with six reform objectives and a 2031 mass-transit ambition. The VAGO audit found that the most consequential action plan items, network design, planning guidance, the infrastructure investment pipeline, require a government decision that the department has not been given. The Legislative Council in March 2024 ordered the Bus Reform Implementation Plan released; the department produced some documents in September 2025, three years after the relevant consultation closed, but withheld the Implementation Plan itself under executive privilege. Victoria pays CDC, Dysons, Kinetic and Ventura roughly $1.7 billion across 2023-25 for 366 routes, 6,000 kilometres, and 114.9 million passenger trips in 2024-25. The department's own patronage estimate may undercount the network by up to 30 million trips per year, based on VAGO's automated passenger counter comparison.
policies.economic_logic: The 2013 VAGO growth-area transport audit identified approximately $197 million per year in recurrent bus service funding gaps in Melbourne's outer growth areas. RMIT's 2024 research found that apartment numbers grew 88% between 2004 and 2022 while public transport services within walking distance grew just 5%: the Upfield line saw apartment growth of 134% against a 7% service uplift in the same period. The VAGO Bus Plan audit cost $720,000 and took eleven months, against a $1.7 billion biennial payment to bus operators over the same period. The AAA Transport Affordability Index puts annual household car costs at $8,000-$12,000 excluding loan repayments: a household that can drop a car entirely because the bus network makes car-independence viable saves that amount every year indefinitely, which is a larger and more durable cost-of-living improvement than any electoral cycle rebate.
policies.risks_and_failure_modes: The VAGO audit found incremental progress, more than 128 local network upgrades since 2021 adding over 11,000 weekly services, and FlexiRide on-demand services reaching Tarneit North and Melton South, but found that incremental change at this pace cannot deliver the Bus Plan's 2031 mass-transit ambition. The transparency failure is structural: the department accepted VAGO's three recommendations only "in part" or "in principle," which is not a commitment to a number or a date. The specific risk is that the same non-commitment cycle repeats: the department accepts recommendations in principle, publishes no timeline, and VAGO audits again in three years to find the same shortfall. A Fusion MP's tool is to require numbers and dates in writing, attached to PAEC hearing responses that carry ministerial accountability.
policies.evidence_and_precedent: VAGO's June 2026 audit found bus-to-train connection rates of 68-73% for priority bus services connecting to a train within 5-10 minutes in June 2025, despite "buses turning up reliably and on time" ranking as commuters' second highest priority in the department's own consultations. Paris's RATP operates buses on a GPS-tracked real-time timetabling system that adjusts service frequency dynamically based on measured demand at each stop, a model the Bus Plan's data-quality recommendations point toward but do not specify. NYC's Mamdani administration included transit service improvements in its FY2027 budget, explicitly linking the Chief Savings Officer savings mandate to reinvestment in bus frequency and reliability as a cost-of-living measure, the same sequencing Fusion's policy argues for.
policies.implementation_outline: This is a crossbench-leverage policy: the transparency and accountability asks are achievable from one seat; the service investment requires a majority government decision. The Fusion MP uses PAEC to require the Secretary of DTP to table: (1) the Bus Reform Implementation Plan in full, the document withheld under executive privilege despite a standing Legislative Council order; (2) a specific numerical standard for household proximity to high-quality bus services and the current measured gap; and (3) confirmed delivery timelines with first-service dates for each funded Melton South and outer-suburban route. Those three things on the public record are the one-seat deliverable: they turn "we accept the recommendations in principle" into a statement that can be checked against a number and a date. If the department still refuses to produce the Implementation Plan, the Fusion MP introduces a Private Member's Bill amending the Transport Integration Act 2010 to require the Secretary to publish an annual Bus Network Performance Report against a statutory standard, with the standard set in the legislation itself so it cannot be indefinitely deferred.
policies.cost: Orbital bus network capital and recurrent costs need corridor-level appraisal
policies.funding: Test proposed transit funds and any employer levy against revenue, equity and operating costs before committing service levels.
policies.change_summary: Explicitly framed outer-suburban transport reform as car-optional rather than anti-car, with reliable alternatives to compulsory driving.
